headline: Otter AI Can Now Understand Conversations in Over 30 Languages

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Otter.ai makes a computer program that listens to meetings and writes down what people say. This is called transcribing. Now, Otter is getting much better at understanding many languages. Soon it will understand 31 different languages! The coolest part is that if people in a meeting switch languages while talking, like going from English to Korean to Portuguese, Otter can follow along without anyone telling it to change. It figures this out all by itself. This helps people from different countries work together more easily, because language differences will not stop them from understanding each other. Thirteen new languages are ready to use right now, including Chinese, German, and Russian. Fourteen more languages, like Arabic, Hindi, and Thai, are coming soon. The company trained its computer program using lots of real speech and asked people who speak these languages to check if the writing was correct. Otter is also adding new tools to help people get ready for meetings and get helpful tips while they are talking.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Otter.ai, a company that builds AI tools for taking notes during meetings, just announced a big upgrade. Their software can now understand conversations in more than 30 different languages, and it can even follow along when speakers switch languages in the middle of a meeting. For example, if someone starts speaking English, then switches to Korean, then to Portuguese, Otter will keep transcribing accurately without anyone needing to change any settings. This matters because many companies today have teams working together from different countries, and language differences can make meetings confusing or slow. With this update, Otter adds 27 new languages, its biggest expansion so far, bringing its total to 31 languages supported. Thirteen of these languages, including Mandarin Chinese, German, and Russian, are available immediately. The other 14, including Arabic, Hindi, and Thai, will be added soon. To build this technology, Otter created its own speech-recognition models. They trained these models using large amounts of public audio and text, then had native speakers review the results to make sure everything was accurate. This project comes after Otter raised $320 million from an investment group called General Catalyst, and the company has been adding other AI features too, like Work Mode, which helps people prepare for meetings using past notes and files, and Live Assist, which gives real-time suggestions during a live conversation. Altogether, these updates show how AI is becoming a bigger part of everyday work, helping people communicate better across language and cultural barriers.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Otter.ai, a company known for its AI note-taking software, announced an important update this week: it can now transcribe conversations in more than 30 languages, and it can smoothly follow along even when speakers switch between languages mid-conversation. This new feature, called multilingual transcription, detects when someone changes languages and keeps writing down what is said without requiring the user to manually adjust any settings. For instance, in a single business call, someone could speak English, switch to Korean, and then move to Portuguese, and Otter would keep up with the conversation the entire time. This update is especially useful for companies with international teams, where language barriers can make meetings harder to follow and slow down collaboration. To make this possible, Otter added support for 27 new languages, which is the largest expansion the company has made at once. Once fully rolled out, Otter will support a total of 31 languages. Thirteen of these new languages, including Mandarin Chinese, Korean, German, Russian, and Vietnamese, are already available. The remaining 14, such as Arabic, Hindi, Thai, and Hebrew, will be released soon. According to Otter, these new language features run on speech-recognition models the company built itself. The models were trained using publicly available data, and Otter worked with native speakers to check the transcripts for accuracy before releasing them. This expansion comes shortly after Otter received $320 million in funding from General Catalyst, a major investment firm, and reflects the company's push to grow beyond basic transcription services. Otter has recently introduced other AI-powered tools as well. One is called Work Mode, which uses information from past meetings, connected apps, and files like Google Drive documents to help users prepare for upcoming calls. Another is Live Assist, a feature that gives people real-time coaching suggestions while a meeting is happening, based on what has already been discussed and what is currently being said. Together, these updates show how Otter is trying to become more than just a transcription tool, aiming instead to be a complete AI assistant for workplace communication, especially for teams that span different countries, time zones, and languages.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Otter.ai, an AI-powered note-taking company, revealed a major upgrade this week aimed at making its software more useful for international teams. The centerpiece of the announcement is a new multilingual transcription feature capable of following conversations even as speakers switch between different languages in real time. Previously, users might have needed to manually indicate a language change or use separate tools for each language, but Otter's new system automatically detects when a speaker switches languages and continues transcribing seamlessly. In a company's example, a single call could shift from English to Korean to Portuguese, and Otter would track the entire exchange without interruption. This technology addresses a real and common problem for global businesses: language differences can slow down meetings, create miscommunication, and complicate record-keeping when team members speak different native languages. As part of this update, Otter is adding support for 27 new languages, which the company says is its largest language expansion yet. Once fully released, Otter will support 31 languages overall, a significant jump that could make the platform more appealing to multinational corporations and remote teams scattered across different countries. Thirteen of the new languages, including Mandarin Chinese, Cantonese, German, Italian, Russian, Vietnamese, and Polish, are already functional, while 14 more, including Arabic, Hindi, Thai, Hebrew, and Persian, are set to arrive at a later date. Notably, these newly supported languages are powered by speech-recognition models that Otter built in-house rather than relying entirely on outside technology. The company trained these models using publicly available datasets and then collaborated with native-speaking volunteers who reviewed transcripts to verify accuracy, a step that suggests Otter is trying to avoid the common pitfalls of AI mistranslation or poor recognition of accents and dialects. This announcement arrives not long after Otter secured $320 million in funding from General Catalyst, a prominent venture capital firm, signaling that the company has ambitious plans for growth beyond its original transcription service. Indeed, Otter has been steadily rolling out additional AI-driven workplace tools. One recent example is Work Mode, a feature that draws on meeting history, connected applications, and files such as Google Drive documents to help users prepare for upcoming calls by surfacing relevant past information and outstanding tasks. Another is Live Assist, which offers real-time coaching during meetings by analyzing the conversation as it happens and providing timely suggestions. Taken together, these updates illustrate a broader trend in the tech industry: AI companies are racing to build tools that do more than transcribe speech, instead positioning themselves as comprehensive assistants for workplace communication and decision-making, with language accessibility now viewed as a key competitive factor.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Otter.ai, a company best known for its AI-driven meeting transcription software, unveiled a significant expansion of its multilingual capabilities this week, signaling a broader strategic shift toward becoming an all-encompassing workplace AI assistant rather than a narrow transcription tool. The centerpiece of the announcement is a new multilingual transcription feature designed to track conversations fluidly even as speakers alternate between languages within the same meeting. Rather than requiring users to manually indicate which language is being spoken, the system automatically detects language switches and continues transcribing without interruption. The company's own example illustrates the scope of this capability: a single call might shift from English to Korean to Portuguese, and Otter would follow the entire exchange accurately throughout. This kind of seamless, automatic language detection represents a meaningful technical achievement, since most transcription systems historically have been optimized for a single language at a time, and switching languages mid-conversation has been a persistent challenge in speech-recognition technology. The update directly addresses a practical problem faced by increasingly globalized and remote workforces, where teams spanning multiple countries and native languages often struggle with communication barriers during meetings, making accurate record-keeping and follow-up more difficult. As part of this rollout, Otter is adding support for 27 new languages, which it describes as its largest language expansion to date. Once fully implemented, the platform will support 31 languages in total. Thirteen of these languages, including Mandarin Chinese, Korean, German, Italian, Cantonese, Portuguese, Russian, Indonesian, Malay, Dutch, Turkish, Vietnamese, and Polish, are already available to users. The remaining 14, including Swedish, Danish, Finnish, Arabic, Hindi, Thai, Hebrew, Norwegian, Greek, Macedonian, Persian, Czech, Hungarian, and Romanian, are expected to roll out in the near future. Importantly, Otter built these new language capabilities using its own proprietary speech-recognition models rather than depending solely on third-party translation services. The company trained these models on publicly available datasets and then partnered with native-speaking volunteers to manually review transcripts for accuracy, an approach meant to reduce common AI pitfalls such as misinterpreting regional accents, dialects, or culturally specific phrasing. This expansion follows closely on the heels of Otter securing $320 million in funding from General Catalyst, a major venture capital firm, underscoring the company's aggressive push to scale its operations and diversify its product offerings beyond basic note-taking. In recent months, Otter has introduced several other AI-powered features aimed at reshaping how people prepare for and participate in meetings. Work Mode, for instance, draws on meeting history, connected applications, and documents such as Google Drive files to help users prepare for upcoming calls by surfacing relevant past conversations and unresolved action items. Live Assist, another recent addition, provides real-time coaching during live meetings, analyzing the flow of conversation and offering contextually relevant suggestions as discussions unfold. Collectively, these developments reflect a wider trend within the AI industry, in which companies are competing not just on raw transcription accuracy but on building comprehensive ecosystems that support decision-making, preparation, and cross-cultural communication in professional settings. As businesses continue to operate across borders and time zones, tools like Otter's multilingual transcription may increasingly be viewed as essential infrastructure rather than optional conveniences.
